sources.title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment — researchImpacts
sources.text: The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted. By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

sources.title: STDCE-1 — Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 — approach
sources.text: Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

sources.title: BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids - II — researchImpacts
sources.text: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning.

sources.title: Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures — hypothesis
sources.text: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.

sources.title: STDCE-1 — Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1 — researchImpacts
sources.text: Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

sources.title: ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames — researchImpacts
sources.text: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing). The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion. The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard. Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

sources.title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets — researchImpacts
sources.text: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

sources.title: No partial-gravity combustion data yet
sources.text: PSI currently holds no combustion data at lunar or martian gravity. The challenge notes that microgravity and normal-gravity results can bound intermediate gravity levels, and that E-FIELD (PSI-22) mimicked partial gravity with ion-driven forces. Limitation: Bounding is not interpolation: behaviour at 1/6 g may not lie between the two cases for every metric.

sources.title: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative
sources.text: Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better in microgravity than in normal gravity. Limitation: Specific materials and geometries; flow and O2 per test partly only in raw files for BASS.

top_passage.text: The experimental setup in the microgravity science glovebox consisted of an apparatus with a flow duct with integrated nozzles, cameras, and fuel delivery systems. Fuels tested included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene mixtures. Each flame was ignited in a controlled co-flow air environment, with burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s. Fuel flow rates were adjusted to identify the smoke point, marked by the flame's transition to emitting soot. Data such as flame lengths were recorded using still and video cameras. Measurements included flame height, radiative heat losses, and co-flow air velocity distributions.
